questions.question: Distinguish the cash budget from the projected statement of comprehensive income, giving items unique to each.
questions.expected_answer: The projected income statement forecasts PROFIT on the accrual basis: income earned against expenses incurred, so a credit sale enters in the month of sale, and depreciation and bad debts appear because value is consumed and losses expected. The cash budget forecasts the BANK BALANCE on the cash basis: a credit sale enters only when the debtor pays, depreciation never appears because no money moves, and bad debts show up merely as cash that never arrives. Unique to the cash budget: capital contributed, drawings, loan receipts and repayments of capital, fixed asset purchases, VAT paid over. Unique to the projected income statement: depreciation, bad debts and accrual portions of expenses. Test every line by asking whether it moves money this month, earns or consumes value this month, or both.

questions.question: Build March's collection from debtors given: sales 40% cash and 60% credit; debtors pay 50% in the following month less 5% discount, 30% in the second month, 15% in the third, and 5% is written off. Credit sales were R108 000 (Dec), R120 000 (Jan) and R150 000 (Feb), with March sales of R300 000.
questions.expected_answer: From February: 50% of R150 000 = R75 000, less the 5% settlement discount = R71 250. From January: 30% of R120 000 = R36 000. From December: 15% of R108 000 = R16 200. Total collection from debtors in March = R123 450. Adding March's cash sales of 40% × R300 000 = R120 000 gives R243 450 of trading receipts. Three disciplines: the discount applies only to the 50% portion that earns it; each month draws on three different months' sales, so the schedule is laid out as a grid; and the 5% written off never enters the cash budget — it appears in the projected income statement as bad debts.

questions.question: Explain how a business can forecast a healthy profit and a dangerous cash deficit in the same month, and describe how variance analysis should be read afterwards.
questions.expected_answer: Timing. Sales made on credit in March earn profit in March but arrive as cash in April and May; the stock supporting them was paid for in February; wages are paid in March; and an asset may be bought for cash in March. Profit says the business is trading well while the bank balance cannot cover next week's wages — both are true, and a good answer names the specific items rather than saying 'one is cash and one is profit'. Afterwards, variance analysis compares budget to actual item by item, stating the figures, the rand and percentage difference, and whether it is favourable or unfavourable, then interpreting: an unfavourable sales variance may mean weaker demand or an over-optimistic budget; a favourable expense variance is not automatically good, since advertising underspent may explain the sales shortfall beside it. Variances must be read together, and the monthly comparison is what makes a budget a control rather than a wish.
